output.title: When a retainer quietly becomes a blank cheque
output.body:
The quiet cost of an open-ended retainer is not the monthly fee. It is the way undefined work keeps expanding until nobody is sure what was actually being bought.

If you are a 1–10 person business, the real question is usually simpler: which one recurring workflow is dragging on your time every week? Repetitive customer questions, manual invoice work, or neglected leads are the usual suspects. In the representative scenario we use at Bareni, that can mean 8–10 hours a week of repeated work. That is not a market statistic, just a practical owner problem.

The bounded alternative is a one-time diagnostic. We look at one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed pilot with clear scope, price, and measures. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. The point is to avoid paying forever for a vague promise that keeps changing shape.

This also keeps control where it belongs. Your data, automation, and API accounts stay in your name from the start. Retainer support is optional, not a trapdoor. And for money movement or other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. No machine gets to sign the cheques; that would be a bad office policy.

If the workflow is high-sensitivity, or if it depends on things we do not build, we say so plainly. The practical next step is to write down one recurring workflow, its current weekly cost, and the one outcome that would justify a pilot. Then you have something real to compare against a retainer.
